3' hydroxy groups act as 'proof reading' signals for DNA polymerases. If a mismatch occurs in base pairing, the 3'OH group will not be incorporated into the chain and therefore the DNA polymerase will stop growing. However, RNA polymerases do NOT have any proof-reading ability. This is why chemicals such as AZT (which mimic the base thymine) are so effective at terminating growing viral DNA chains - they cannot be recognised by the DNA polymerase and therefore the DNA polymerase will continue growing down the template strand until it reaches a normal base which it can incorporate. Promoters are cis-acting elements that recruit RNA Polymerase II and other transcriptional factors which then assemble at the site of the promoter where transcription will occur.  Enhancers are cis-acting elements that recruit proteins that interact with the transcriptional complexes to increase transcription.  Both promoters and enhancers are located on the same DNA molecule as the gene they control.  Transcription Factors (TFs) are a family of proteins that bind to specific DNA sequences and regulate transcription by recruiting RNA Polymerase II or inhibiting its recruitment to a particular gene.  TFs often work together in complexes called cooperative complexes.  Some TFs only have a role in activating genes (activators), others only have a role in repressing genes (repressors).  Some TFs can be both activators and repressors depending on the context.  TFs can also act combinatorially, meaning that two different TFs working together can result in a much stronger effect than either one working alone.  TFs can also synergize, meaning that the presence of one TF can make another TF more effective.  TFs can also antagonise each other, meaning that the presence of one TF can inhibit the action of another TF.  TFs can also work in a hierarchical manner, meaning that one TF can recruit other TFs to assist it in activating/repressing a gene.  TFs are important because they provide a flexible way of controlling gene expression, allowing cells to respond quickly and appropriately to changes in their environment.  TFs are also involved in many cellular processes such as development, differentiation, and apoptosis.
